guideTitle: 6 Best Cast Iron Skillets Under $20 in 2026
metaTitle: 6 Best Cast Iron Skillets Under $20 in 2026
metaDescription: Six small pre-seasoned cast iron skillets under $20, from 6-inch single-serve pans to 8-inch workhorses, compared on handles, spouts, lids and care.
introParagraphs: At this budget, cast iron means small. Every skillet here is a compact pan between 6 and 8 inches, which is exactly the right size for one or two portions, a pair of eggs, a seared chop, or a side that goes straight to the table.

That size comes with real advantages for new owners. A small pan is lighter to lift, quicker to heat, and easier to wash and oil than a 12-inch giant, which makes it a forgiving first piece of cast iron. We evaluated each pick from listing specs and buyer feedback themes, focusing on handle shape, pour spouts, included lids and what the maker says about seasoning.
The tradeoff against spending more is cooking area, not quality of iron. Read on for what each pan does well, where it falls short, and which kind of cook should pick it.

products.name: Lodge 8-Inch Pre-Seasoned Cast Iron Skillet
products.description:
The classic Lodge 8-inch is the benchmark for small cast iron. It arrives pre-seasoned and ready to cook, with a teardrop handle that suits most hands and thick iron that holds heat for a proper sear. The maker lists it as PFAS-free, and it shares the heat-retention reputation that made the brand a default choice.

Simplicity is also what limits it. There are no pour spouts, so draining liquid means a careful tilt, and the iron needs drying and a thin coat of oil after each wash. It is heavier than a nonstick pan of the same diameter, which you will notice when lifting it one-handed.

Against the Lodge Chef Collection it is plainer, with no spouts and no flared sidewalls, but it is also the most familiar shape to cook on. Against the MOZUVE 6-inch it gives more surface for a pair of eggs. Preheat it gently for a couple of minutes, add oil, and let it rest before you move food so the crust releases on its own.
products.bestFor: First-time cast iron buyers who want a proven shape in a manageable size.

products.name: Lodge Chef Collection 8-Inch Skillet
products.description:
Where the standard Lodge keeps things bare, the Chef Collection adds thoughtful details. The sidewalls are shaped so a spatula slides under food, the handles are ergonomic, and generous pour spouts sit on the rim to help drain fat or sauce. It is seasoned with natural vegetable oil, which gives an easy-release finish.

You pay for those details with the same compact footprint. Eight inches is small for family meals, and bare cast iron still needs the usual care of drying, oiling, and avoiding long soaks. The extra shape work will not change how heavy the pan feels, since the iron mass still sits in your wrist.

Compared with the plain Lodge 8-inch, the spouts and sidewalls are real daily conveniences, especially for pan sauces. Against the Utopia with its lid, you lose steaming ability but gain better pouring. Pour from the spout nearest your dominant hand, wipe out the pan while it is still warm, and use a mitt on the handle every time.

products.name: Utopia Kitchen 8-Inch Skillet with Lid
products.description:
A lid changes what a small skillet can do. The Utopia includes one, so you can steam vegetables, reheat leftovers without drying them out, and braise a thigh in the oven. The pan arrives seasoned with vegetable oil and is listed for stove, oven, grill and campfire use.

The set has limits. The size is too small for family sized braises, two portions crowd the surface, and no handle cover is included, so you need your own mitt for both the pan and the lid. The lid also adds one more piece to wash and dry, since leftover moisture is the usual cause of rust.

Compared with the Lodge 8-inch, you get lid versatility for the same footprint, but the Lodge has a longer track record and a teardrop handle. Next to the Vesici pair, it is one pan with a cover rather than two pans without. Dry both pan and lid fully on a warm burner, store them with a paper towel between so air can circulate, and handle the lid knob carefully since it heats up.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want to steam, reheat and braise small portions.

products.name: MOZUVE 6-Inch Cast Iron Skillet with Drip Spouts
products.description:
The MOZUVE is the smallest cooking pan in this group, and that is its identity. Six inches across, it holds one egg, one fillet, or a single serving of cornbread. Drip-spouts let you pour off fat cleanly, and the listing says it is seasoned with 100 percent vegetable oil with no synthetic coatings.

The small surface crowds quickly if you try to cook more than one item, and the listing does not describe the handle shape, so you cannot judge grip in advance. It is a pan for one person or a side dish, not a replacement for a full skillet.

Compared with the Lodge 8-inch, it is lighter to hold and uses less oil, but it handles fewer foods at once. Against the Vesici pair, it adds the spouts and a smaller footprint but loses the second pan. Heat it a little longer than you think, use only a little oil for eggs, and wipe the pan out with a paper towel while it is still warm to protect the seasoning.
products.bestFor: Solo cooks who want one egg or one fillet at a time.

products.name: Vesici 2-Piece 7.9-Inch Cast Iron Skillet Set
products.description:
Two pans in one box is the pitch of the Vesici. The listing describes a pair of 7.9-inch skillets with drip-spouts, suited to a single-person breakfast, snacks, or sides, and calls them sturdy, durable and good at storing heat. Two pans mean you can cook a main and a side at once, or serve one pan each.

What the listing leaves out is detail. There is no seasoning description in the text here, no handle shape, and no weight, so you should assume a first wash and seasoning check before cooking. Two pans also double the oiling and drying chores, and they take more cupboard space than a single pan.

Versus the Lodge Chef Collection, you get twice as many pans but fewer documented design features. Versus the MOZUVE, the pans are larger. Season them lightly on arrival, rub a thin film of oil over both, and bake them upside down in a warm oven so the coating cures evenly before the first meal.

specList.label: Chemistry

products.description:
The EWFEN positions itself on cleanliness and a smooth finish. The listing says it is pre-seasoned with natural vegetable oil, rated heat-safe to 500F, and free of PFOA and PTFE. A smooth interior is meant to aid release and cleaning, which can be welcome in a small pan that does breakfast duty.

There are gaps. It is less established than Lodge, it has no spouts or assist handle on the rim, and it needs the same drying and oiling as any bare iron. The temperature rating is a ceiling, not an invitation to run it empty at full heat.

Compared with the Lodge 8-inch it gives you a similar size with a documented heat rating, while the Lodge brings the stronger name. Against the Utopia, you do not get a lid. Preheat on medium rather than high, test with a drop of water, and add food only once the pan is evenly hot to avoid sticking in the first few uses.

buyingCriteria.explanation: Every skillet here is between 6 and 8 inches, so decide how many items you cook at once. The MOZUVE at 6 inches fits one egg or one fillet, while the Lodge, EWFEN and Utopia at 8 inches handle a pair. The Vesici at 7.9 inches each gives you two pans. If you regularly cook for three or more, this size will feel cramped.

Pre-seasoned means a baked-on layer of oil that makes the pan usable immediately. The Lodge, Utopia and EWFEN all arrive seasoned with vegetable oil. That layer is thin, though, and it improves with every use rather than being finished on day one. Expect the first few meals to stick a little and cook fatty foods early on.

A small pan lives or dies by how it handles when full. The Lodge Chef Collection adds ergonomic handles and generous pour spouts, the MOZUVE and Vesici add drip-spouts, and the plain Lodge relies on a teardrop handle. Cast iron handles get hot, so every option needs a mitt. Spouts matter most if you drain grease or make pan sauce.

A lid turns a skillet into a small pot. The Utopia includes one for steaming and reheating, and no other pick here does. If you want to braise or reheat leftovers without drying them, that matters more than a spout. Without a lid, a plate or foil can fill in.

Cast iron is dense, and even small pans feel heavy compared with aluminium. The 6-inch MOZUVE is the easiest to lift, the 8-inch Lodge feels more substantial, and the listings give no weights. If you have weak wrists, favour the smallest size or a pan with an assist handle.

Bare iron rusts if it stays wet. Wash with hot water, dry on a warm burner, and rub a thin film of oil on the surface. Avoid long soaks and acidic simmering in a young seasoning. Two pans, like the Vesici set, double the routine, so factor in your patience.

howWeEvaluated.title: Size fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched pan diameter to the portions each listing describes. The MOZUVE leads for single servings, the Lodge and EWFEN for a pair of eggs, and the Vesici for two-pan cooking. A small pan was not penalised for being small.

howWeEvaluated.title: Handling features
howWeEvaluated.description: Pour spouts, ergonomic handles and sidewall shape were compared. The Lodge Chef Collection scored highest, with the MOZUVE and Vesici adding spouts, and the plain Lodge and EWFEN offering fewer helps. We drew on listing details and common buyer complaints about drips.

howWeEvaluated.title: Seasoning and surface
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at what each maker says about the finish. Lodge and Utopia name vegetable oil seasoning, EWFEN mentions a smooth finish and chemical-free claims, and the Vesici listing says little. Documented finishes earned credit.

howWeEvaluated.title: Versatility
howWeEvaluated.description: A lid, a heat rating or an outdoor use claim adds range. The Utopia stands out for its lid, the EWFEN for its 500F rating, and several picks mention camping. We kept the claims tied to what the listing states.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ease of ownership
howWeEvaluated.description: Weight, number of pieces and cleaning steps affect whether the pan gets used. The MOZUVE is simplest, while the Vesici pair doubles the care. We assumed a beginner who has never seasoned a pan.

faq.q: Is a small cast iron skillet worth buying?
faq.a: Yes, if you cook for one or two or want a pan for eggs and sides. Eight inches is plenty for a pair of eggs, and six inches suits one fillet. For family dinners you will want a larger skillet later.

faq.q: Do I need to season a pre-seasoned pan?
faq.a: Not before the first use, because the factory layer is ready to cook on. It still improves with use, so cook fatty foods first and rub a thin film of oil on after every wash. The Vesici listing says little about seasoning, so a light home seasoning is sensible.

faq.q: Can I wash cast iron with soap?
faq.a: A little mild soap is fine on a modern pre-seasoned pan, followed by thorough drying. Avoid dishwashers and long soaks, which cause rust. Dry on a warm burner and wipe with a thin film of oil, then store the pan somewhere dry with the lid off so air can reach the iron.

faq.q: What is the difference between PFAS-free and PTFE-free claims?
faq.a: The Lodge listing says PFAS-free, and the EWFEN says PFOA and PTFE free. Both are the maker's statements about the coating, and traditional cast iron has none beyond seasoning oil. Read them as reassurance about the coating, not as a quality score or a guarantee of how well the pan will sear or release food.

faq.q: Why does food stick in my new pan?
faq.a: The seasoning layer is thin at first and builds over time. Preheat gently, use enough oil, and wait for food to release before turning it. Starting with fatty foods like bacon helps the surface mature.

Iron is magnetic, so cast iron generally suits induction, but the listings here do not mention it. Check the maker's guidance, lift rather than slide the pan to protect the glass, and use a mitt as the handle gets hot.

faq.q: Which of these is the lightest to handle?
faq.a: The 6-inch MOZUVE has the smallest mass and is the easiest to lift. The 8-inch pans feel more substantial, and none of the listings publish weights. If you have weak wrists, favour the smaller size.
